\chapter{Speaking to Somebody}
\label{ch:hi-sambodhan}
\hlchaptermodality{105}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can address somebody by name, in speech and on paper, and write a short message to a named reader.}

Write the whole message to a named reader from a purpose cue alone: the opening line that names them, two sentences underneath, and your own name at the foot.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Mīrā jī]{\hi{मीरा} \hi{जी} — putting a name in front of somebody}

\label{lesson:HI-C97-naam-ji}



\begin{quote}
Say the small word you learned that turns a bare \textbf{\hi{हाँ}} into a polite one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मीरा} \hi{जी}}
\textbf{\hi{मीरा} \hi{जी}} (\emph{Mīrā jī}) — how you address somebody called Mira.

A name, then \textbf{\hi{जी}}. That is the whole of it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the word you already had, in a new position}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you say} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
\hi{जी} \hi{हाँ} & makes a yes polite \\
\hi{मीरा} \hi{जी} & makes a name an address \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{जी}} has been in your mouth since the early chapters, doing politeness work after a yes. Behind a name it does the same work in a different place: it turns somebody being \emph{talked about} into somebody being \emph{talked to}.

Hindi has no separate ending for this the way some languages do. \textbf{The position is the grammar} — the name comes first, \textbf{\hi{जी}} follows it, and nothing else in the sentence changes.

It works for anybody you would use \textbf{\hi{आप}} with, which is most people you have not known since childhood. With a close friend or a child, the bare name on its own is the ordinary thing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \hi{मीरा} \hi{जी}
  \item \hi{अरुण} \hi{जी}
  \item which of the two words carries the respect
  \item what changes in the rest of the sentence (nothing)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you address somebody called Mira? Which word goes first, the name or \textbf{\hi{जी}}? Where had you met \textbf{\hi{जी}} before this?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[priya]{\hi{प्रिय} — the word a letter starts with}

\label{lesson:HI-C97-priya}



\begin{quote}
Address somebody called Mira out loud. Today's word does the same work on the page.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{प्रिय}}
\textbf{\hi{प्रिय}} (\emph{priya}) — \emph{dear}.

It goes \textbf{before} the name: \textbf{\hi{प्रिय} \hi{मीरा}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the opposite side of the name}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{written} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
\hi{प्रिय} \hi{मीरा} & \hi{मीरा} \hi{जी} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{One goes in front and one goes behind}, which is worth noticing because it is the kind of thing a reader gets backwards once and then remembers. \textbf{\hi{प्रिय}} is an adjective describing the person, so it leads; \textbf{\hi{जी}} is an honorific attached to them, so it follows.

\textbf{\hi{प्रिय}} belongs to writing. Saying it to somebody's face is the sort of thing that would make them look up. A note, a card or a letter is where it lives, and that is the one place this chapter is heading.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \hi{प्रिय} \hi{मीरा}
  \item the spoken version of the same address
  \item which of the two words comes before the name
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{प्रिय}} mean? Which side of the name does it sit on? Is it for speaking or for writing?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sambodhan]{\hi{संबोधन} — two openings, one question to pick between them}

\label{lesson:HI-C97-repaso-sambodhan}



\begin{quote}
Say the word a written message opens with, and say which side of the name it sits on.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the two side by side}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where} & \textbf{what you say or write} \\
\midrule
out loud & \hi{मीरा} \hi{जी} \\
on paper & \hi{प्रिय} \hi{मीरा} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One question chooses between them: \textbf{are you speaking or writing?} Answer it and the opening is decided, along with which side of the name the extra word goes on.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what the two have in common}]
Neither of them changes the sentence that follows. Hindi marks address by putting a word beside the name rather than bending anything, so whatever you were going to say stays exactly as it was and the opening sits in front of it.

That is worth holding on to, because a great deal of what this track has taught you does the opposite. Endings agree, vowels shorten, verbs bend for who is speaking. \textbf{Address is the corner of the grammar that asks nothing of the rest of the sentence.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the opening for somebody called Arun, out loud
  \item the opening for a note to Arun
  \item which of the two puts its extra word after the name
  \item what changes in the sentence after the opening (nothing)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which question picks the opening for you? Which of the two belongs to the page rather than the mouth? What does the rest of the sentence do when an opening is added? (Nothing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[priya Mīrā,]{\hi{प्रिय} \hi{मीरा} — a page with somebody at the top of it}

\label{lesson:HI-C97-sandesh}



\begin{quote}
Say the written opening for a reader called Mira. Then recall the upright stroke that closes a Hindi sentence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing: the three parts, with the model in front of you}
A short Hindi message has three parts stacked down the page:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{प्रिय} \hi{मीरा},}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{नमस्ते।} \hi{कल} \hi{मिलते} \hi{हैं।}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{— \hi{अरुण}}
\end{quote}

Copy it once, keeping the three parts on their three lines.

Every word of that is something you have written before. \textbf{What is new is the arrangement} — two sentences you could already produce, lifted onto a page that now has a reader at the top of it and a writer at the bottom.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why the opening earns its own line}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{part} & \textbf{what it carries} \\
\midrule
\hi{प्रिय} \hi{मीरा}, & who is being written to \\
\hi{नमस्ते।} \hi{कल} \hi{मिलते} \hi{हैं।} & what is being said \\
— \hi{अरुण} & who is writing \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The opening is not a sentence and takes no \textbf{\hi{।}} after it. A comma does that work, which is the one piece of punctuation here that behaves the way English punctuation does.

The two sentences underneath keep their \textbf{\hi{।}} each. Being inside a message leaves the end of a Hindi sentence exactly as it was.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the three parts of a message? Which of them takes a comma rather than a \textbf{\hi{।}}? Who goes at the foot of the page?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[priya Aruṇ,]{No model — a whole message to a named reader}

\label{lesson:HI-C97-sintesis-sandesh}



\begin{quote}
Close the preceding lesson. Wait ten seconds. Name the three parts of a message to yourself without looking at them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing: produce the message from the cue alone}
There is no Devanagari model and no romanized answer below. Keep only this cue:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Write to Arun. Greet him, then say you will meet tomorrow. Put your own practice name at the foot.}
\end{quote}

Write all three parts from memory. Then compare in four separate passes:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item three parts present, in order;
  \item the comma after the opening and one \textbf{\hi{।}} after each sentence;
  \item spelling and vowel marks;
  \item the name at the foot.
\end{enumerate}

Choose the first differing pass, repair only that dimension, and stop.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which part of a message names the reader? Which takes a comma rather than a \textbf{\hi{।}}? Whose name sits at the foot?

This is the short message the A1 writing task asks for in outline. It is not a timed mock, and its length is well under what that task sets.
\end{tcolorbox}
